title: Chem-PerturBridge: a harmonized compendium of small molecule perturbation transcriptomic effects
claim: Matched cross-source conditions agree only weakly in fine-grained magnitudes, but beat peer baselines and show strong direction agreement and retrieval.
layout: 16 heatmap panels in 4 rows by 4 columns, observed versus three baselines
description: A dense grid of 16 triangular heatmap matrices, arranged as four boxed rows labeled a–d, e–h, i–l and m–p. Each row is a different metric: DEG logFC Spearman, DEG logFC direction agreement, cross-dataset logFC retrieval, and direction retrieval. Within a row, the columns are Observed, Source centroid baseline, Source peer baseline and Target peer baseline. Each matrix compares datasets (L1000 Phase I and II, Tahoe-100M, CIGS-MCE, CIGS-TCM, sci-Plex). Cells carry numeric values on a yellow-to-dark-blue colormap, with a colorbar beside each panel. The eye goes first to the dark-blue cells in the centroid-baseline and observed panels, then compares them with the pale target-peer panels at the right of each row.
caption: logFC agreement and retrieval across Chem-PerturBridge. DEG-restricted logFC correlation is generally weak in absolute terms and often falls below the within-dataset same-context different-compound centroid, but exceeds individual peer baselines in most pairs. Cross-dataset logFC direction agreement is substantially stronger and usually outperforms all baselines. Crossdataset retrieval ranks the matched compound above the target-peer baseline in all pairs, but below the averaged centroid, which itself ranks highly. Retrieval on signed directions is close to magnitudes (mean rank 0.67 vs. 0.68), exceeding the target-peer baseline in every pair. Each panel is a datasetby-dataset matrix over the resources in Table 1. a–d) DEG-restricted (adj. p < 0.05) gene-wise Spearman correlation of log fold-changes. e–h) Signed direction agreement on genes differentially expressed in both signatures. i–l) Cross-dataset logFC retrieval of the matched partner against same-context different-compound distractors, under cosine similarity. m–p) The same retrieval on signed directions, sign(logFC). Retrieval is reported as normalized best-positive rank, where higher is better; 1.0 is the best. Within each row, panels report the cross-dataset score and the remaining three baselines: the source-side centroid baseline, individual source peers and individual target peers. Perturbagen-clustered bootstrap confidence intervals for panels a–p are reported in Tables 6, 7, and 12.
abstract: Large perturbation models require training data encompassing chemical, cellular, and assay diversity. Current transcriptomic resources for small-molecule modeling, however, are fragmented across technologies, metadata conventions, controls, doses, and preprocessing pipelines. We introduce Chem-PerturBridge, a harmonized multi-dataset resource comprising over 37k compounds, 136 cellular contexts, and 1.25M transcriptomic samples across eight assay types, with standardized identifiers, metadata, and replicate-aware condition-level effects. We use the resource to evaluate matched-condition agreement across datasets and replicate agreement within datasets. Matched same-compound conditions show weak absolute agreement in fine-grained $\mathrm{logFC}$ rankings and magnitudes across most dataset pairs. However, they generally exceed individual same-context different-compound signatures, while often falling below the smoothed centroid of such signatures. Same-compound retrieval is above chance in all pairs. $\mathrm{LogFC}$ direction agreement is high in absolute terms, and exceeds both baselines in most cases. We further evaluate Chem-PerturBridge as a pretraining resource for compound representation learning. Under a compound-held-out OP3 evaluation split, embeddings pretrained on Chem-PerturBridge improve over L1000-only embeddings, Morgan fingerprints, chemical language model embeddings, and the descriptor-free OP3 baseline across metrics. An extensive molecule-holdout evaluation across 11 datasets further shows that models trained on Chem-PerturBridge outperform or match those that are not. Chem-PerturBridge therefore supports both diagnostic evaluation of cross-dataset signature agreement and model-oriented reuse of heterogeneous perturbation transcriptomic data.
